runs.text: Homem que ſe rapa, & deixa o

lines.note: Tonjeija denotes a person who shaves his head and leaves worldly life; the Portuguese relative clause continues on the next row.
Mundo completes the renunciation of the world. The final rounded o corrects OCR munde; this short continuation belongs to Tonjeija.
Tonji, alternatively tonxi, is sudden death, explained by niwaka ni shisuru. The worn n and j support Tonji rather than the OCR's Toiiji.
Subitanea and arrebatada both qualify morte as sudden or abrupt; they complete the preceding entry rather than introducing another sense.

runs.text: Tonji, zuru, ita. i, Tongiacu ſuru.

lines.note: Tonji, tonzuru, tonjita is equated with tongiaku suru, being attached to or covetous of something. The Portuguese construction continues below.

runs.text: com affeição entregue a algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The person is affectionately attached to some object. Vt introduces the example whose divided Ta- continues as tacara, riches, on the next row.
Tacara ni tonzuru describes craving riches, matching cubiça and affeição. The physical Ta-/carani division is retained.
The gloss completes attachment to riches, then vonna ni tonzuru introduces an analogous desire for women; the initial v is part of the historical spelling.
Dar-se or entregar-se a mulheres explains the previous example. Saqe begins the following example concerning drink and food.
Saqe, xocubut ni tonzuru means being wholly devoted to eating and drinking. Xocubut retains the historical checked final t before ni.
Mer completes comer across the physical break; beber completes the paired activities of eating and drinking.

Tonjiqi is gluttony or appetite, paraphrased by shoku wo musaboru, craving food. Reinspection after the supplied NINJAL lexical checkpoint confirms the damaged q and its descender, rather than OCR Tonjioi; muſaboru replaces maiſaboru. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); this scan decides the transcription.
Tite completes apetite, specified as appetite for eating. The short row is a genuine continuation of Tonjiqi.
Tonna is equated with niwakana, sudden or unexpected. Niuacana is supported by the printed u and the Portuguese repentina, correcting OCR Ninacana.
Tonni is the adverb suddenly. Adu. is the italic grammatical label; the second Portuguese expression de repente is divided after re-.
Pente completes de repente, repeating the suddenness sense of Tonni rather than adding an independent entry.

runs.text: Senhor de algũa terra, ou que tem cria

lines.note: Tono is a lord of land or a person with retainers. The printed cria continues as criados without a supplied line-end hyphen.
Dos completes criados, followed by income as another mark of lordship. The paragraph sign then introduces the distinct use meaning husband.

runs.text: Palaura de que vſão algũas molheres honradas

lines.note: The husband sense is identified as a word used by some respectable women. The worn initial h of honradas is read with the Portuguese context, not as OCR bonradas.
Falando de seus maridos completes the usage restriction: these women use tono when speaking of their husbands.
Tonobara is described as an esquire below a fidalgo or knight. The line ends with visibly divided fidal-, not the OCR period.
Go completes fidalgo, followed by caualeiro. The comparison concerns social rank in the preceding Tonobara definition.
Tonodono denotes lords with vassals; Item then introduces another sense whose explanation follows on the next row.

runs.text: Caſas de ſenhores, ou fidalgos que estão juntas.

lines.note: The second Tonodono sense is the adjacent houses of lords or noblemen. The plural casas governs the final juntas.

runs.text: Certa laya de penas de hum paßaro

lines.note: Tǒ no fa denotes feathers of a particular bird, valued for arrows. The final s of penas is severely abraded but a residual stroke remains after a; the plural boas below also supports the adopted reading. The exact bird is not identified beyond its printed name.

The bird is called Tǒ; its feathers are suitable for arrows. Enlargement shows a downward caron rather than the OCR grave. The name retains the italic type visible within the Portuguese explanation and is marked separately for whole-word typeface review.
Tonoi means night watch or watchers. Tonoibaramaqi introduces the armour worn by these guards, with armas divided across the physical break.
Mas completes armas; the line specifies armour worn by the watchers. The reference is protective equipment rather than weapons held in the hand.
Tonoibito is a watchman, equated with banxu and glossed Vigia. The damaged Portuguese word is clarified by the repeated vigias above and below.
Tonoidoqi denotes the soldiers’ shout while at war. Grita and soldados correct OCR Orita and saldados; the following lines explain the occasion.

runs.text: na guerra com que acodem todos às tardes com

lines.note: The soldiers respond together in the evening while campaigning. The sentence continues with their drawn swords and the preceding signal.

runs.text: as Catanas nuas depois de ouuirem o ſinal da

lines.note: The soldiers hold naked or drawn catanas after hearing a horn signal. Nuas and ſinal correct the garbled aias and ſinol without modernizing the Portuguese spelling.
Buzina completes the horn signal that occasions the collective cry. It is a short continuation of the Tonoidoqi description.

runs.text: Vestido de que vſão eſtas vigias

lines.note: Tonoimono is clothing used by the watchers; the following line explains its additional function during the night watch.

runs.text: de noite em lugar de cama, ou cobertor, & q̃

lines.note: The garment serves at night instead of a bed or cover. The abbreviation q̃ introduces the final clause and is not expanded in the transcription.

runs.text: fazem leuar ao lugar da vigia.

lines.note: The watchers have this garment carried to their watch station. This completes the description of Tonoimono as portable bedding or covering.
Tǒ no tçuchi is glossed Aluayade, white lead. The caron and the separated tçuchi are retained rather than replaced with modern Japanese spelling.
Tonozzucuri refers to building important residences. The scan supports principaes, correcting the OCR peinãpaes; the alternative paços follows below.
Ou paços identifies palaces or grand residences as the alternative expression for the houses being built.
Tonpi is illustrated by tonpi wo utsusazu, acting without delay. The Portuguese Depreßa supplies the practical meaning; the historical Japanese phrase is retained.
Sem tardança completes the explanation as without delay. It belongs to the preceding example, not the following entry on mental quickness.
Tonqi is explained by hayaqi qi, quick disposition, and by vivacity or an alert mind. The last Portuguese adjective continues below.
To completes esperto; habil adds ability. Tonqina fito then illustrates an alert or capable person, whose Portuguese gloss continues below.
Vivo, esperto and habil complete the characterization of the Tonqina fito as lively, quick and capable.
Tonſacu denotes an impromptu work or saying, made suddenly. The compact derepente is retained as printed.
Tonſacuna fito is someone who speaks or acts promptly; the Portuguese relative clause continues on the following row.

runs.text: faz as couſas de preßa, & ſem muito cuidar.

lines.note: The person does things quickly and without much prior thought. This is an indented continuation of the Tonſacuna fito gloss, not a fresh entry.
Tonſocu means something hurried or accomplished quickly. The scan supports n in the headword rather than OCR m; preſ continues as presteza without a supplied hyphen.
Teza completes presteza; ligeiramente adds the sense of speed or lightness. The row belongs to the Tonſocu definition.
Tonſocuna is the corresponding adjectival form, referred back by Idem to the preceding hurried or quick sense.
Tonſocuni is the adverbial form of the same expression. Adu. supplies the grammatical category without repeating the whole definition.
Tonxa is rapid copying, explained by niwaka ni utsusu. The visible cedilla in vtçuſu and l in Tresladar correct OCR vtcuſu and Trestadar.

runs.text: preſſa o Foquequiǒ repartindo as folhas por

lines.note: The Lotus Sutra, named Foquequiǒ, is copied quickly by distributing its leaves. Enlargement shows two long-s types in preſſa and a caron, not a tilde, over the book title’s final o. The title retains the surrounding italic type; its Japanese identity is recorded separately for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: muitos eſcriuaẽs fazẽ iſto por algũ defuncto

lines.note: The leaves are divided among many scribes, who perform the copying for a deceased person. The abbreviated fazẽ and algũ remain unexpanded.
The copying takes place at funeral rites or burial. The printed double r in enterramento corrects the single-r OCR reading.
Tonxei, alternatively tonjei, is leaving worldly life, paraphrased by yo wo nogaruru. The Portuguese begins with shaving the head.

runs.text: ſe. i, Deixar a caſa, ou o mundo. Vt,

lines.note: Shaving is explained as leaving one’s house or the world. The example visibly begins Ten-, an anomalous vowel beside the headword Tonxei; it is retained rather than silently corrected.
Ten-/xeino mi to naru means becoming a person who has renounced worldly life. The Portuguese describes becoming shaven in that manner; the full desta replaces OCR dest-.
Maneira completes desta maneira. The visible e corrects OCR mancira and closes the renunciation example.
Tonxi, alternatively tonji, repeats the sudden-death entry, paraphrased by niwaka ni shisuru. The Portuguese adjective is divided after su-.
Bitanea completes subitanea. Tonxi xerareta, alternatively xita, gives the past-tense example, translated by morreo across the line break.
Reo completes morreo: the person died suddenly. The scan supports ſubitanea rather than the OCR’s extra c in ſubitancea.
Tonxin is a covetous or craving heart, explained by musaboru kokoro. The Portuguese begins the description of an avaricious person.
Rento completes avarento, joined by covetous and sensual. The final upright S. labels written usage rather than belonging to the italic gloss.
Tonxu is a deferential formula expressing courtesy and humility. The scan supports Palaura, correcting OCR Paſaura.

runs.text: que ſe eſcreue no cabo das cartas. Vt,

lines.note: The formula is written at the close of letters. Qiô- begins the example repeated across the line break.
Qiô-qiô tonxu is the formal epistolary expression. Both qiô syllables have circumflexes; the second is not the OCR caron.
Tonyocu is equated with yocuxin and glossed as avarice or covetousness. The headword’s desire sense accords with the surrounding ton- entries.
Toppa, alternatively toppana, characterizes a heedless or disordered person. The visible spacing of a tabalhoado is retained as printed.
Desatentado supplies the alternative characterization, and toppana mono illustrates the same kind of person. Idẽ refers to the preceding definition.
Toppo here means walking alone, explained by fitori ayomu. The printed ayomu is retained rather than modernized to ayumu.
Hum soo completes the idea of one person going or walking alone; it belongs to the first Toppo entry.

runs.text: O eſtar farto, ou ter comido tè mais

lines.note: A second Toppo entry describes satiation or having eaten to one’s limit. The two p letters and final s of mais correct OCR Toupo and mair.

runs.text: não poder, ou eſtar cheo, ou com ſobejo viço

lines.note: The description continues with being unable to eat more, being full, or having excessive plenty and indulgence.
Toppono amarini introduces the consequence of excessive fullness; the Portuguese begins com o demasiado across the line break.

runs.text: maſiado comer, & fartura, ou viço. Vt,

lines.note: Masiado completes demasiado: excessive eating, satiety or indulgence. Vt introduces a full Japanese example on the following line.
Toppono amarini mono wo suru means doing something out of excessive satiation or indulgence. Fazer begins the explanatory Portuguese clause.

runs.text: algũa couſa com que hum moſtra eſtar muito

lines.note: The action demonstrates that someone is very full or satiated. The sentence is continued on the following physical row.

runs.text: farto, ou cheo, ou com ſobigidão dalgũa couſa,

lines.note: The person is full, supplied abundantly with something, or indulged. The historical ſobigidão is retained rather than replaced by a modern paraphrase.
E viço completes the list of fullness and indulgence associated with the action described above.
Tǒqe denotes this house or family. The example Tǒqeno begins a phrase completed by fito on the next row.
Fito completes Tǒqeno fito, a person of this house or family, precisely matching the Portuguese gloss.
A second Tǒqe denotes the current year’s crop or sowing. The capital T is clear in the scan, correcting OCR Fǒqe.

runs.text: no de arroz que eſtà ainda em eſpiga no cam-

lines.note: No completes anno; the entry concerns rice still standing in ears in the field. Campo is divided across this line and the next.
Po completes campo. Tǒqe ga yoi, alternatively varui, describes the crop as good or bad; the translation continues below.
Sementeira boa ou ruim completes the contrast of a good and a poor crop; it is not a further headword.
Toqe first means coming untied, then melting; the following example uses toquru. The second Portuguese infinitive is divided after Der-.
Reterſe completes derreterse. Rǒ ga toquru gives melting wax; cera is divided after ce- at the end of the row.
Ra completes cera. Kokoro tokete mono wo yuu illustrates speaking with one’s reserve dissolved, followed by the divided Portuguese falar.

runs.text: lar ſẽ ter pejo; ou muito familiarmente.

lines.note: Lar completes falar: speaking without embarrassment or very familiarly. The gloss explains the figurative opening of the heart in the preceding example.
Toqeai gives the reciprocal or collective melting of several things. The printed Derreterenſe is preserved without regularizing its inflection.

runs.text: jũtas como caramelos, ou neues de muitas partes.

lines.note: The things melt together, exemplified by ice formations and snow from several places. This is a continuation of Toqeai rather than a new entry.
Toqei is the hare’s narrow path, equated with usagi no michi. The Portuguese begins its physical description among grass and scrub.

runs.text: lebre por antre as eruas, ou mato. ¶

lines.note: The hare’s path runs through grass or brush. Daizǒ begins the elephant example continued on the next page; the separate bottom toqeini is a catchword, not another body row.
The catchword anticipates toqeini aſobazu on f514. Its o is worn and open, but it is retained as a separate repeated catchword rather than appended to Daizǒ or joined to the signature.
